description: Variables, types, and print() — your first real Python.

screens.body:
Python is a programming language — a way to write instructions a computer follows. It's famous for reading almost like English, which makes it a friendly first language.

Python runs your code line by line, top to bottom. The simplest thing you can do is print() — it shows text on the screen so you can see what's happening.
screens.heading: Meet Python
screens.keyPoint: Python reads almost like English and runs top to bottom.

screens.body:
A variable is a name that holds a value — like a labeled box you put things in. You create one with the = sign: name on the left, value on the right.

Python figures out the type by itself. You never have to declare "this is text" or "this is a number" — it just knows.
screens.heading: Variables are labeled boxes
screens.keyPoint: name = value stores a value under a name.

screens.body:
Any text wrapped in quotes is a string — single or double quotes both work. Strings are how Python handles words, sentences, and messages.

You can glue strings together with the + sign. Programmers call that concatenation — a fancy word for "sticking text together".

check.question: Which of these is a string?

screens.heading: Strings: text in quotes
screens.keyPoint: Text in quotes is a string; + glues strings together.

screens.body:
Whole numbers like 19 are called ints (integers). Numbers with a decimal point like 19.5 are called floats.

The math operators work like you'd expect: + - * /. One quirk: / always gives you a float, even when the answer is whole — 4 / 2 gives 2.0, not 2.

check.question: What type is the result of 7 / 2?

screens.heading: Numbers: ints and floats
screens.keyPoint: ints are whole numbers, floats have decimals; / always returns a float.

screens.body:
A boolean is a value that's either True or False — nothing in between. Booleans answer yes-or-no questions in your code: is the user logged in? Is the task done?

Watch the capital letters: Python only accepts True and False with a capital first letter. true with a lowercase t is a completely different (and broken) thing.
screens.heading: Booleans: True or False
screens.keyPoint: Booleans are True or False — capital first letter.

screens.body:
Python is strict about mixing types. "I am " + 19 crashes, because you can't add text and a number. You have to convert first: str() turns things into text, int() into whole numbers, float() into decimals.

Not sure what type something is? The type() function tells you. It's like asking Python "hey, what is this?"

options: Crashes — can't add str and int
check.question: "5" + 5 does what?

screens.heading: Converting between types
screens.keyPoint: Use str(), int(), float() to convert; Python won't mix types silently.

screens.body:
f-strings let you drop variables straight into text using {curly braces}. Just put an f before the opening quote — Python fills in the values for you.

They're much tidier than gluing with + and str(). Once you learn f-strings, you'll use them everywhere.

options: Puts the value of name into the text
check.question: What does f"Hi {name}" do?

code.snippet:
name = "Roli"
age = 19
print(f"{name} is {age} years old")

screens.heading: f-strings: tidy messages
screens.keyPoint: f"..." with {braces} drops variables into text.

screens.body: Keep exploring with the official Python docs — they're free and written by the people who make Python. The Python tutorial (docs.python.org/3/tutorial/) walks through everything here and more, and the built-in types page (docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html) is the full reference for strings, numbers, and booleans.
screens.heading: Go deeper
screens.keyPoint: The official docs are your best next stop.

title: Python Basics
